summary:
Illes Balears stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. The statute applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, and no source in the inventory records a Balearic deviation from that framework.

Article 43 allows any person aged 16 or over to request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, without prior surgical reassignment and without the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. The right to the registered change is grounded in the free development of personality under article 10.1 of the Constitution. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision Human Rights Watch reported as contentious when the Congress passed the law.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination: the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. That contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime; the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

The statute defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, and obliges the collection of discrimination data broken down by those causes. It also bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expands assisted reproduction rules, provides parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and imposes anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation. The administrative self-declaration route under Article 43 places Spain alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.
tangentialFactors:
Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime is grouped with Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay, which operate comparable routes to legal gender recognition.

A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change. The finding is a dated baseline that predates Ley 4/2023 and cannot be read as a measure of opinion under the current statute.

The United Kingdom's move towards biological-sex lines in single-sex spaces, applied restriction by restriction rather than as a blanket prohibition, is the principal comparative divergence a trans visitor should expect against the Spanish position.

The two enforcement decisions cited are the clearest evidence of how the gender-identity aggravation operates in practice, and both were handed down outside Illes Balears, in Vigo and Valencia respectively.
localsOnly:
Employers, service providers and public authorities in Illes Balears are bound by provisions that sanction discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, void discriminatory contract clauses, and require discrimination data collection broken down by those causes. The statute also mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances.

Healthcare, employment and housing discrimination are covered expressly, alongside anti-LGBTI protections that Human Rights Watch described as strengthened when the Congress passed the law.

Residents are affected by the ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, the expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and strengthened sexuality education in schools.

The law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and sets the conditions under which a person from age 12 may obtain recognition of their gender mention; a person aged 16 or over may request rectification on their own entry without a legal representative.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records Balearic-level implementation detail: processing times at Balearic Civil Registry offices, which office serves which municipality, and whether any additional documentary requirement is applied locally are unresolved and not sourced here.

The enforcement decisions available for the gender-identity aggravating circumstance come from other parts of Spain, in Vigo and Valencia. Whether the aggravating circumstance has been applied by a Balearic court is unresolved on the present sources.

Practical conditions of facility access in Balearic municipalities, including any municipal rules that depart from the civil-registry marker basis, are not sourced. The inventory contains no regional enforcement or complaint data for Illes Balears.

The 2016 survey evidence on public opinion predates Ley 4/2023 and is not evidence of current Spanish opinion.
